title: Zoya and the Biased Bus
markdown:
Zoya buzzed with excitement, notebook open. Student council project: find the best way for students to get to Northwood High. “This will be fascinating,” she told Pebble, the ancient tortoise. Pebble blinked, his shell a map of weathered lines, and offered a slow nod. Ms. Lin watched from her doorway, a knowing smile like the first hint of dawn. “Patience. Discoveries take their time.”

No owl gathered a crowd. The oak rustled because oaks do that.

“First,” Zoya declared, tapping her pen, “I’ll poll everyone at the main gate in the morning. Quick and easy. A clear majority.”

She returned later, bounce gone, replaced by a bewildered frown. “This is odd.” She flipped through her notes. “It looks like everyone takes the bus. Eighty percent. But I know half my friends bike, and plenty walk. It doesn’t add up.” She had asked the first hundred students she saw by the main gate. It seemed like a lot. Something felt off, a melody slightly out of tune.

Lin approached, graceful as a falling leaf. “What troubles you? Your brow is a ploughed field.”

“My survey. It’s all buses. Is Northwood a depot with classrooms attached?”

Lin chuckled, a hidden-stream sound. “Consider the sun. When it shines brightest at noon, are students rushing toward school, or heading home? And where does the afternoon bus pick up? Same spot as the morning drop-off?”

Zoya paused. Morning. Main gate. “But that’s where everyone comes.”

“Everyone who arrives at that time, at that place, yes. Imagine a forest. If you only counted squirrels at your bird feeder, would you know the whole wood? You would miss the ones gathering nuts deeper in, or foraging by quiet streams.”

The analogy clicked. Zoya looked at Pebble, who was making his slow steady way toward the bike racks, entirely absent from her morning count. He was not at the main gate. He was just moving.

“You mean my sample is biased. Not a fair picture of everyone.”

“Precisely. A specific group, a specific moment. A tide pool is not the ocean.”

Determination surged, a sapling through stone. She spent the rest of the day observing. Bike racks at 8:15, then again at 8:45. The walking path at 8:30. The bus loop after school. Data from every angle, like a crow collecting shine from different parts of a meadow. She even counted Pebble once, as a joke, and wrote tortoise / not a student in the margin so she would not accidentally include him in the percentages.

By day’s end she had a fuller picture. The bus was popular, but so were biking and walking, their numbers shifting with time and neighbourhood. She presented the findings, voice clear. “My first results were wrong because my sample was biased. I only asked students who arrived at the main gate in the morning. It didn’t represent everyone.”

Lin nodded, eyes warm. She did not begin a lecture on informed decisions. “A small group under specific conditions can look like the whole truth. A representative sample is slower. It is also truer.”

Zoya beamed. Pebble gave a slow satisfied blink. Lin did not ask what other wonders waited beyond the gate. Zoya stapled the morning-gate sheet behind the all-day sheet so the mistake would stay visible, a cautionary appendix, and walked Pebble home past the bike racks that her first graph had pretended did not exist.
